notes.1a: Candidates were expected to recognise that collusion is an agreement between firms; maybe to fix prices, maybe to fix output by quotas, maybe both. It could be an agreement on restricting advertising. It is most likely to occur when there are a small number of firms, where it is easy to monitor and/or where products are similar. A number of candidates began their answer with a tautology, stating that ‘collusion is a collusion between firms’. Most candidates mentioned an agreement but a surprising number did not answer the second part of the question which asked when collusion is most likely to occur.
notes.1b: Many candidates answered this question without any reference to Table 1. Instead they made general statements about price fixing or price discrimination. Better candidates used the table to analyse some changes to suggest whether Procter and Gamble had benefitted from price fixing. They cited, for example, that earnings in 2010 were down compared with 2009, but they rose between 2006 and 2000; that the dividend rose throughout the period; that sales fluctuated but the overall trend was up. The best candidates commented that it was difficult to come to an overall �PAGE�29 9708 Economics June 2013 conclusion, for example because there is no information about prices, only about overall earnings, which may be partly the result of cost changes.
notes.1c: This section was answered well by most candidates. They were not required to restrict their answer to the case of Procter and Gamble and were able to consider the advantages of integration, for example, the benefits of ordering, the supply chain, improvements in administration, economies of scale, specialisation and the use of resources.
notes.1d: For this section it was important that candidates used the information in the article. There was some good analysis of the article and relevant conclusions were drawn. Candidates recognised that although earnings were down in the last year, they may have been down even more if there had been no collusion. The collusion may, therefore, be regarded as being against the public interest. However, better candidates recognised that there was no information about cost saving, nor about rivals’ prices/profits/ costs and, therefore, that there was not enough evidence to conclude that collusion was definitely against the public interest in contrast to other firms’ behaviour. Further evidence was also used to weaken the argument that Procter and Gamble was working against the public interest and was indeed working in favour of the public interest. This included the facts that Procter and Gamble invests in research, that it gets top place in a stated list for its innovations, that it has brand names that are popular with the public and that its packaging was reduced to avoid waste. Section B - Essays
notes.2a: Many candidates explained the term utility and elaborated the principle of diminishing marginal utility as they were asked. However, while many also stated the equi-marginal utility equation it was not always developed to explain how a change in the price of one good would lead to a re- allocation of consumer expenditure to restore the equilibrium. The question also required candidates to analyse how a change in income might affect the allocation. This part of the question was often not answered while other candidates confused a change in income with a change in the price of a good – although of course such a change would affect real income. As a result, too much time was spent developing the idea of income and substitution effects while the effect of an income change on the demand curve was omitted. The better candidates did develop an explanation but in terms of budget lines rather than a demand curve. Very few tried to analyse how a change in income would have a different effect on the demand for a normal good than for an inferior good.
notes.2b: This section usually resulted in descriptive answers of various measures, typically progressive taxes, transfer payments and subsidies. The more rigorous answers suggested support and training to get people into work or into better paid jobs; they also analysed the effect of minimum wage legislation. The most notable weakness was the lack of any evaluation or assessment of how well the various measures might achieve the objective of a more equal income distribution.
notes.3: This question was answered by most of the candidates from some Centres but ignored completely by the candidates from other Centres. Some who answered the question repeated, often haphazardly, all they could remember about wage theory frequently spending too much time on economic rent and transfer earnings. More relevant answers began by developing an explanation of the marginal revenue productivity model in perfect competition. These reports have stressed in the past that, while it is possible to answer such questions as this with reference only to demand and supply diagrams and analysis, the higher marks are awarded to candidates who use marginal revenue productivity analysis. Relatively few, however, produced a clear, comprehensive and well-organised explanation. Since governments and trades unions were mentioned in the question many candidates simply wrote about these institutions fixing minimum wages. Stronger candidates did analyse market imperfections more fully and produced diagrams and some analysis of monopsony and bi-lateral monopoly. Sadly, there was often no real link to the context of the question and a focus and explanation of how the theory might be ‘adapted’ was notable by its absence. �PAGE�30
notes.4a: The purpose of the first part of the question was to require candidates to explain why economic growth and inflation might occur at the same time. Candidates needed to show that they understood what the question meant by a rapid rate of economic growth and a high rate of inflation and then to explain why these two situations could occur simultaneously. Good answers demonstrated that candidates understood that economic growth involved an increase in aggregate demand, which caused an increase in national income in the form of real gross domestic product. There would be an expansion of productive potential and a shift of the production possibility curve to the right. A number of candidates distinguished between actual growth and potential growth, and many explained the component parts of aggregate demand. Their answers demonstrated that they understood that if aggregate demand was in excess of aggregate supply it could cause inflation. There was often a good use of appropriate diagrams to support the explanation.
notes.4b: The purpose of the second part of the question was to ask candidates to discuss what policies might be used by a government to control the rate of inflation in an economy. The better answers to this question discussing policies from both a demand-side and a supply-side perspective. On the demand side, candidates included both fiscal policies, including reducing the level of government spending and increasing taxation, and monetary policies, including both reducing the money supply and increasing the rate of interest. On the supply side, candidates instanced policies such as increasing competition in markets to bring about a greater degree of efficiency. Poorer answers did not demonstrate what effect the policies might have but simply listed alternative policies; others confused expansionary and contractionary approaches. Better answers discussed the various advantages and disadvantages of the policies before concluding which of the policies would be likely to be the most effective. It is important that candidates do fully address the command word used in a question.
notes.5a: The purpose of the first part of the question was to ask candidates to explain what changes might occur both to the age distribution and to the occupational structure of a population as an economy changed from a developing one to a developed one. In considering the changes in the age distribution of a population, candidates mentioned the likely changes in the birth rate, the death rate and the infant mortality rate. The better answers commented on the fact that the average age of a population would increase as an economy changed from a developing to a developed status. In explaining the changes in the occupational structure, candidates suggested that there would be a movement away from employment in the primary sector towards employment in the secondary and tertiary sector. Unfortunately, some candidates did not read the question carefully and wrote either about the changes in the age distribution or about the changes in the occupational structure, but not about both.
notes.5b: The purpose of the second part of the question was to ask candidates to consider whether information about a high rate of unemployment and a dependency on international trade was sufficient to indicate whether that country could be classed as developing or developed. Most candidates suggested that both of these situations could apply to either a developing or a developed country and that other information would be required in order to decide whether a country was developing or developed. There was some good discussion of the other criteria that could be used to reach such a judgement. Better candidates drew their argument to a conclusion.
notes.6a: The question required an analysis of what might cause an increase in unemployment. Most candidates dealt with equilibrium unemployment and analysed situations relating to frictional, structural, seasonal and regional types of unemployment. Better answers recognised that the fundamental cause of longer-term unemployment was linked to the business cycle and explained how job losses were linked to disequilibrium between aggregate demand and aggregate supply. The best answers analysed and contrasted Keynesian demand- deficient theory with that of supply side policies, explaining how the latter had been recognised as a valid solution to long-term unemployment through retraining, the use of up-to-date technologies and a curbing of the powers of trade unions to increase wages. �PAGE�31
notes.6b: Some of the better attempts discussed the effects of unemployment on the economy through an analysis of its different impacts on individuals, firms, governments and the economy. The obvious socio-economic impacts on society were explained – loss of earnings, low self-esteem, family breakdown and increasing crime culminating in a falling standard of living. The impact on government finances was usually explained involving loss of tax revenues (fewer in work) but increased spending on welfare benefits for the unemployed. They concluded that increasing unemployment affected all forms of planned government expenditure and tended to increase budget deficits, and added to government debt. The best answers concluded that potential outputs of goods and services that might have been enjoyed by consumers were lost forever due to unemployment. This “cost” to the economy represented the difference between actual and potential GNP which tended to widen during economic recessions. Hence governments needed to take an active management of the macroeconomy on both demand and supply sides.
notes.7: When attempting a discursive subject such as this question about efficient resource allocation, candidates must heed the advice printed in the syllabus concerning command words. To discuss an opinion “arguments for and against should be considered leading to a conclusion”. Candidates are also advised that when discussing an opinion they should “support it with evidence”. Better answers used this kind of framework to explain how the market works under private enterprise based on the price mechanism, consumer sovereignty and profit maximisation. To judge whether this economic system was efficient both productive and allocative efficiency needed to be explained. Most candidates explained adequately that economic efficiency was only obtainable under perfect competition for a firm making normal profit and producing where price equals marginal cost (allocative) and at the lowest minimum average cost (productive). Fewer candidates adequately explained the reality of imperfect competition where, say, a monopoly maximises profit where marginal cost equals marginal revenue but charges price above marginal cost and supplies where total average cost is above its minimum point. Such a situation would not achieve either allocative or productive efficiency. Many used labelled diagrams to illustrate these differences and to explain the abnormal profit that could be made in imperfect competition. The best answers developed the argument further to explain how a market system rarely leads to social efficiency because the marginal social benefits do not equal marginal social costs. They explained that due to profit seeking, firms in all forms of imperfect competition are concerned only with private costs even though many activities incur external costs which fall on third parties. To illustrate this, examples of negative externalities were provided and these were contrasted with positive externalities where marginal social benefit exceeds marginal social costs. Sound conclusions were given by the better candidates who also explained that a purely market system would never provide public goods at the most desirable or optimal levels. Therefore, a mixed economy, they suggested, was essential, with government involvement, to deal with market failure because of the “free rider” principle arising from non-excludability and non-rivalry of some goods and services. Arguments were usually made for government provision of merit goods, such as health facilities, and discouragement of the consumption of demerit goods, such as cigarette smoking, through indirect taxes and direct controls. �PAGE�32
notes.key_messages:
• Candidates need to read the question carefully and direct their knowledge to the particular phrase
and question asked.
• Evaluative and discussion questions always need a ‘conclusion’ or a statement indicating what the
candidate believes.
• It is important that candidates fully address the command word used in a question.
notes.general_comments:
There were some good answers to this paper and those candidates are to be congratulated on the use of
their studies to achieve such marks. It has, however, been mentioned in previous reports that candidates
risk not achieving as high a mark as their knowledge would allow them simply because they do not read the
question carefully and do not use and direct their knowledge to the particular phrase and question asked.
No further knowledge would be required to achieve a higher mark in these circumstances; a re-organisation
and a better presentation of the material is all that is required. For example, in Question 3, candidates often
did not explain clearly how the theory might be ‘adapted’. Two different versions of the theory were
presented and the reader was left to deduce what had changed. In Question 5, part (a) candidates omitted
any reference to occupational structure, and in part (b) candidates did not draw a conclusion to their
argument nor relate their answer to the question about unemployment and international trade. Question 6
asked about an increase in unemployment – candidates did not comment on how any change in employment
might occur. They merely described different types of unemployment in a static situation. It would take little
ingenuity to adapt such knowledge and postulate how a change might have occurred that caused a particular
type of unemployment. Lastly, evaluative and discussion questions always need a ‘conclusion’ or a
statement indicating what the candidate believes – such a statement can be a preface to the answer rather
than an addendum but it needs to be made somewhere. All too often candidates merely presented material
and left the reader to decide what the candidate believed.
